node-1.label: Patient presented with stridor, increased work of breathing, and supplemental oxygen requirement

node-2.label: A man presented to the emergency department on transfer from an outside hospital after falling with an e-cigarette in his mouth several hours earlier; he did not remember the exact cause of the fall and believed he may have lost consciousness

node-3.label: Physical examination in the ED showed diffuse supraglottic edema most severe in the epiglottis, arytenoids, and aryepiglottic folds, which obstructed a view of the true vocal cords

why.why: CT showing glottic and supraglottic swelling without fractures, together with direct laryngoscopy showing diffuse pharyngeal and supraglottic mucosal edema with sloughing most severe in the epiglottis, provides direct support for thermal/chemical mucosal burn from the e-cigarette. Both the Radiologist and Laboratory Physician explicitly interpret these findings as consistent with e-cigarette-related airway burn. Bronchoscopy was not performed, so subglottic/tracheobronchial involvement remains unverified, but the supraglottic findings are sufficient to raise confidence from 0.72 to 0.86.

CT shows no fractures, and direct laryngoscopy reveals diffuse edema with sloughing rather than a focal hematoma or laceration. Expert analyses state that the lack of fractures reduces traumatic injury and that the diffuse pattern is not consistent with isolated blunt trauma from the fall. These findings refute airway trauma from the fall, lowering confidence from 0.18 to 0.05.

The diffuse supraglottic edema with sloughing and the absence of an infectious prodrome argue against acute infectious epiglottitis. Expert analyses specifically note that the diffuse pattern and lack of infectious prodrome make epiglottitis less likely, especially given the more consistent alternative mechanism of e-cigarette-related mucosal burn. Confidence is therefore lowered from 0.10 to 0.03.
